lead: This week the Great Fast walks with Abram. Today God calls him to leave everything on the strength of a promise, and in John a man who has waited thirty-eight years is told to stand up. The second reading shows the opposite of that trust, Achan’s hidden theft and its bitter end in the Valley of Achor. In the epistle Paul grieves for his own people and insists that God’s word has not failed. Both main readings begin with a word from God to someone who has nothing to offer in return.

set: Genesis 1–11 tells of a world spreading away from God, and it closes with Babel, where people said, “let us make a name for ourselves” (11:4). Now God says to one man that he will make his name great (12:2). Abram’s father Terah had left Ur for Canaan and stopped at Haran (11:31), and Abram is called from there. He has no child, for Sarai is barren (11:30). That makes the promise of a great nation seem impossible from its first word.
str: vv. 1–3: the call and the promise: a land, a people, a name, a blessing.
vv. 4–5: Abram goes, with Sarai, Lot and all they have.
vv. 6–9: through the land: Shechem, then between Bethel and Ai, with an altar at each of the first two stops, and on toward the Negeb.
kw: Two short Hebrew words open the story of Israel. The second adds force and is hard to translate: “go, you yourself”. Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator, took it to mean “go for your own good”.
The root “bless” comes five times in vv. 2–3. In Genesis, blessing means life, fruitfulness and peace given by God. Abram receives it so that it may pass through him to others.
Abram owns none of this land, and yet he builds altars in it (vv. 7–8). His first act in the promised land is worship.
vv: Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
The list moves inward: country, clan, home. Each step costs more than the last. God does not name the land yet: he says only, “that I will show you”.
in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
This is the widest line in the chapter. The call of one man is for the sake of all the families scattered at Babel. St Paul reads it as “the gospel beforehand”, and quotes it in Galatians 3:8.
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him;
Abram asks nothing and says nothing. The next thing we learn is his age, seventy-five, which tells us that this call does not come too late for anyone.
ch: The Catechism sees in this call the beginning of God’s answer to a scattered humanity: God calls Abram “in order to gather together scattered humanity” (CCC 59), and his descendants are the trustees of the promise (CCC 60). Abraham is its great example of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146), as in Hebrews 11:8: he set out, “not knowing where he was going”. Nostra Aetate 4 recalls that the beginnings of the Church’s faith are already found among the patriarchs, Moses and the prophets.

r.h: Do you want to be made well?
set: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a festival John does not name. The pool lay near the Sheep Gate, north of the Temple. Excavations near the Church of St Anne have uncovered a large double pool of the right period, which fits John’s description well.

The oldest manuscripts have no explanation of the moving water. A later addition, found in some copies, says that an angel stirred it, and many Bibles omit this as v. 4; the verse numbers of the NRSV and the POC differ here. John’s story depends only on what the sick man says in v. 7.
str: vv. 1–5: the place and the man, ill for thirty-eight years.
vv. 6–9a: the question and the word: he stands and walks.
vv. 9b–13: it is the sabbath: questions about the mat.
vv. 14–15: Jesus finds him in the Temple.
vv. 16–18: “My Father is still working”, and the dispute deepens.
kw: The word comes again and again in the passage (vv. 6, 9, 11, 14, 15). It means sound and healthy. The whole story turns on it.
A poor person’s pallet. Mark uses the same word for the paralysed man let down through the roof (Mark 2:4). What once carried this man he now carries.
The verb of v. 17. Jesus answers the charge of working on the sabbath by speaking about the work of his Father.
vv: Do you want to be made well?

Jesus speaks first; the man has asked for nothing. The question is not a foolish one. After thirty-eight years a person can stop hoping. The man does not answer yes. He explains why it has never happened: “I have no one” (v. 7). The Lord then becomes that someone.
See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you.
Jesus looks for him a second time, because the bodily cure is not the whole gift. See the question below on sickness and sin.
My Father is still working, and I also am working.

Jewish teachers of that age also reflected that God keeps the world in being even on the sabbath. Jesus places his own work beside the Father’s. That is why John says the claim went further than the sabbath: he was “making himself equal to God” (v. 18).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and that he gives its true meaning (CCC 2173; see also 582). John’s phrase “the Jews” in vv. 10–18 means here the authorities in Jerusalem who opposed him, not a whole people: the man, the disciples and Jesus himself are Jews, and the Church firmly rejects any blame laid on the Jewish people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). St Augustine took the five porticoes as a figure of the five books of Moses, which show us our sickness and lead us to the healer (Tractates on John 17; in substance).

qa: Does this mean that sickness is a punishment for sin?

No. In John 9:3 Jesus says of the man born blind, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned”. The word in 5:14 is addressed to this one man and warns of something worse than illness: to lose what God has given. The Church does not teach that each illness comes from a person’s own sin (see CCC 1502–1505).
study: What has God asked me to leave behind in this Great Fast, and have I gone “as the Lord had told” me?
Is there a place in my life where I have stopped hoping? How would I answer if Jesus asked, “Do you want to be made well?”
